entities.summary: Truce/Treaty of Vilna or Truce/Treaty of Niemieża was a treaty signed at Niemieża near Vilnius on 3 November 1656 between Tsardom of Russia and Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, introducing a truce during the Russo-Polish War (1654–67) and an anti-Swedish alliance in the contemporaneous Second Northern War. In return for ceasing hostilities and fighting Sweden alongside Poland–Lithuania, the treaty promised Alexis of Russia succession in Poland after John II Casimir Vasa's death. The Cossacks under Bohdan Khmelnytsky were excluded from the negotiations, and subsequently supported the Transylvanian invasion on the Swedish side.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Truce of Vilna (1656) marked a significant regional shift in Eastern Europe, as Russia and Poland-Lithuania formed an anti-Swedish alliance during the Second Northern War. This treaty had lasting implications for the region's balance of power.
